Where it began

Kuldeep Yadav was born on 14 December 1994 and grew up in Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh. It was his father who kept him at the game and took him along to a coach. The young Kuldeep dreamed of bowling left-arm fast like Wasim Akram and Zaheer Khan, but he was slightly built, and at the trials his coach noticed that his deliveries were turning sharply without him even trying. So wrist spin it was.

From then on he studied videos of Shane Warne, his new hero, watching the grip, the length and the way he used the crease. He went on to play for India at the 2014 Under-19 World Cup.

The player

His Test debut came against Australia at Dharamsala in March 2017, and he took four wickets in the first innings. He was the first left-arm wrist-spinner to play Test cricket for India. His first five-wicket haul came against the West Indies in 2018, and in January 2019 he took five more at Sydney in his first Test in Australia.

By November 2026 he had played 19 Tests between 2017 and 2026, taking 80 wickets at 23.36 with five five-wicket hauls and a best of five for 40. For a spinner who was often in and out of the side, those are figures to be proud of.

What made him special

Kuldeep's wrist spin and his variations make him hard to read and great fun to watch. He has been a match-winner in the shorter formats too: two one-day hat-tricks, the second making him the first Indian bowler to manage the feat twice, and six for 25 against England in 2018. He was named player of the tournament at the 2023 Asia Cup and he was part of the India sides that lifted the Champions Trophy in 2025 and the T20 World Cup in both 2024 and 2026.

Batting is not really his department, though a best of 40 among his 252 Test runs shows he can hang around when the side needs it.

Away from the middle

Kuldeep is a keen football fan who supports Barcelona, and he has spoken of wanting to start football academies in India one day. In 2025 he started a football channel on YouTube. In the summer of 2026 he joined Yorkshire for a short spell in county cricket.

And finally

He set out to be the next Wasim Akram and ended up as a cricketer in the mould of Shane Warne instead. Most coaches would call that a decent bit of advice.
